items.readable_text:
Content:
A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}: \mathbb R^n \rightarrow \mathbb R^n] is invertible if there is another linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}] such that

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}))=\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{T}^{-1}(\mathbf{v}))=\mathbf{v}]

Content:
for every vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}\in \mathbb R^n.] The transformation of [MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}] is called the inverse of [MATH: \mathbf{T}.] An invertible linear transformation is also called a bijection.

Content:
We have the following theorem regarding invertible linear transformations:

Content:
> If [MATH: T] is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}], then [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is invertible if and only if [MATH: T] is invertible.

Content:
Recall that the invertible matrix theorem in terms of dimension, rank, and nullity states that if [MATH: T] is an [MATH: n \!\times\! n] matrix, then

Content:
> [MATH: T] is invertible [MATH: \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad]
> [MATH: Col(T) = R^{n}; dim(Col(T)) = n = rank(T); Null(T) = {0}; dim(Null(T)) = 0 = nullity(T).]

Content:
In the theorem above, we can make the following swaps, where [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a linear transformation with the standard matrix [MATH: T{:}]
[MATH: Col(T)|= Im(T); rank(T)|= rank(T); Null(T)|= Ker(T); nullity(T)|= nullity(T)]

Content:
As a result, we obtain the invertible matrix theorem in terms of linear transformations:

Content:
> [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is a bijection (invertible) [MATH: Im(T) = R^{n}; rank(T) = n; Ker(T) = {0}; nullity(T) = 0]
> [MATH: \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad] [MATH: T] is invertible

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}: \mathbb R^n \rightarrow \mathbb R^n] is invertible if there is another linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}] such that

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}))=\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{T}^{-1}(\mathbf{v}))=\mathbf{v}]

Content:
for every vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}\in \mathbb R^n.] The transformation of [MATH: \mathbf{T}^{-1}] is called the inverse of [MATH: \mathbf{T}.] An invertible linear transformation is also called a bijection.

Content:
We have the following theorem regarding invertible linear transformations:

Content:
> If [MATH: T] is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}], then [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is invertible if and only if [MATH: T] is invertible.
